decision_titles: FY26 audit results and final audited financial statements
transcript:
DRAFT · MINUTES OF REGULAR MEETING · BURLINGTON ELECTRIC COMMISSION · Wednesday, October 14, 2026

The regular meeting of the Burlington Electric Commission was convened at 5:02 p.m. on · Wednesday, October 14, 2026, at Burlington Electric Department, 585 Pine Street, Burlington, · Vermont, and on Microsoft Teams.

Attendance

 Channel 17 was present to record this meeting. ·  Commissioners Paul Dawson, Ali Kenney, Andy Vota, and Brian Willams were present at · 585 Pine Street. ·  Staff members Paul Alexander, Sami Bousnina, Amanda Hurlbut, Mike Kanarick, Munir · Kasti, Katie Morris, Darren Springer, and Emily Stebbins-Wheelock were present at 585 · Pine Street. ·  Staff member James Gibbons was present via Microsoft Teams. ·  Public members Leendert Huisman and Peter Macausland were present at 585 Pine Street. ·  Public members Jake Day and Jeffrey Koch of KPMG were present via Microsoft Teams.

## 1. Agenda

There were no changes to the agenda.

## 2. Meeting Minutes

There was one proposed change to correct a typo to “Velerity” in the September 9, 2026 minutes.

Commissioner Vota moved to accept the September 9, 2026 minutes pending the typo correction; Commissioner Williams seconded the motion. Vote: 4 ayes 0 nays.

## 3. Public Forum

Peter Macausland addressed the commission noting the importance of public forums and detailed minutes outlining points that were discussed in the meeting so that other public members can benefit from the discussion.

Leendert Huisman addressed the commission regarding the Velerity report, specifically its pyrolysis proposal for reducing greenhouse gas emissions from the McNeil facility.

Mr. Huisman noted the report is a year old but still important. From informal web research, while the results may be incomplete or inaccurate, Mr. Huisman noted that the information found was not reflected anywhere in the report. The report states a 60% efficiency for syngas as a fuel for generating electricity; this is the high end of the 30 to 60 percent range typically seen, and Mr. Huisman was unsure why Velerity chose the top of the range.

Pyrolysis produces a variety of volatile gases, either during the process or when syngas is burned. The report mentions only nitrogen oxides. Mr. Huisman noted a main concern of CO2 per kilowatt hour; the key measure of greenhouse gas performance is kilograms of CO2 per kWh. The report cites the current McNeil figure of 1.36 kg CO2/kWh. For pyrolysis to be worthwhile, it needs to beat straight wood burning, but the report gives no figure for the pyrolysis option, so it’s unclear whether it would be higher, slightly higher, or much higher. Mr. Huisman acknowledged the report only outlines options and is not a full life cycle analysis.

Mr. Huisman noted that whoever proposes to build a pyrolysis system should provide: the efficiency of burning syngas in their specific setup, all volatile emissions beyond nitrogen oxides, and the CO2 per kWh emitted.

## 4. KPMG Audit Presentation

Amanda Hurlbut, BED Controller, introduced Jake Day and Jeffrey Koch of KPMG to present the preliminary results for the FY26 audit. KPMG has been working with the department since early August. The audit is substantially complete, with a few outstanding items before it can be finalized. Ms. Hurlbut thanked the finance and accounting team for their work during the audit and throughout the year.

Jeffrey Koch noted that audit quality is KPMG’s top priority. The firm is integrating AI and other technology into its audits. Mr. Koch described a progression from human auditors using technology as an assistant, to the current “human-led, agent-operated” audit, to an “AI-powered, human- assured” audit beginning in 2027. Professional judgment and accountability remain with the audit team.

KPMG is forming an opinion on the financial statements, including the fiduciary funds. It does not form an opinion on the effectiveness of internal controls. No uncorrected misstatements have been identified to date. Remaining items include legal letter updates, management’s representation letter, the finalized City OPEB report, and resolution of some outstanding questions. The audit is expected to be finalized on time within the next few weeks, subject to completion of those items.

Jake Day noted there were no difficult or contentious matters requiring outside consultation and no actual or suspected fraud involving management or employees with significant roles. The engagement letter has been provided to management. The representation letter will be finalized when the final report is ready. KPMG affirmed it is independent as of October 14, 2026. The auditor’s report will include an emphasis-of-matter paragraph, consistent with prior years, referring to Note 1. The department’s statements present only the portion of the City of Burlington’s activities attributable to the department. The opinion is not modified. There are no changes to existing accounting policies; the department adopted two new standards: GASB 103 (financial reporting model improvements) and GASB 104 (disclosure of certain capital assets). There were no indicators of management bias, and presentation and disclosures conform with US GAAP. The department uses reputable custodians for investment valuation. The City engages a qualified actuary for the pension liability, which is allocated proportionately to the department, and KPMG uses its own actuarial specialist to assess it.

Required supplementary information (MD&A) was not audited, but KPMG performed limited procedures and found no contradictions with management’s responses or the audited statements. Required inquiries were distributed to the board in advance.

Commissioner Vota moved that the commission enter executive session pursuant to 1 V.S.A. statute 313(a)(3) for the purpose of discussing the evaluation of public employees in connection with findings and recommendations contained in the KPMG audit; Commissioner Dawson seconded the motion. Vote: 4 aye 0 nay. The Burlington Electric Commission entered executive session at 5:24 p.m.

Commissioner Vota made a motion to exit executive session; Commissioner Williams seconded the motion. Vote: 4 aye 0 nay. The Burlington Electric Commission exited executive session at 5:41 p.m.

Commissioner Williams made a motion to accept KPMG's report of audit results for the fiscal year ending June 30th, 2026 as presented and to authorize issuance of the final audited financial statements upon completion of the outstanding matters identified tonight with any change that is material to the results reported back to the commission before issuance. Commissioner Vota seconded the motion. Vote: 4 aye 0 nay.

## 5. Monthly Impact Minute

Emily Stebbins-Wheelock, CFO and Manager of Strategy and Innovation, introduced Sami Bousnina, BED’s new Financial Analyst.

Sami Bousnina joined BED in July 2026 and has been preparing the financial review for the past two months, doing survey work, creating an update of our five-year forecast, and performing the regular forecast.

## 6. Commissioners’ Corner

Commissioner Williams raised a comment regarding the use of AI in the city and if there was a city- wide AI policy. After attending a PMI conference last week where AI was a major topic, Commissioner Williams asked if BED has set an AI policy. Commissioner Williams noted the use of AI could be mainly a source of time savings and efficiency rather than a flashy tool, paired with guardrails so it makes people’s jobs easier while keeping use controlled. Williams acknowledged this may not be an item to address this year, but supports setting a policy and getting started. Commissioner Williams looked for a City AI policy and could not find one.

General Manager Darren Springer responded that a relatively new City AI policy exists as of September 2026, and BED is adopting it with perhaps minor changes. BED has an AI chatbot, “Sparky,” now available at a kiosk near the customer care window. BED’s IT director describes it as more of a widget than a true AI chatbot, though it provides some AI capability on the BED website. Internal uses considered acceptable include proofreading and designing documents. The City and BED discourage unchecked written work products generated by AI. The City and BED primarily use Microsoft products (Teams, Copilot). Some staff also use tools like ChatGPT or Gemini. BED expects to set tighter controls on who uses which tools, such as whether a professional license is needed, steering people toward Copilot (or free licenses where available) and using other tools only when necessary, with some form of request process.

## 7. GM Update

General Manager Darren Springer provided updates to two BED projects; both the battery and solar canopy projects are close to the permitting stage (the solar canopy is slightly closer). SunCommon will manage the canopy permitting. A team meets weekly with Kearsarge Energy on the battery siting and process. Once the PPA is finalized, the battery will be submitted to the Public Utility Commission for a 90-day waiting period. The goal is for both to be built and operational next year, at different points in the year.

The wood pyrolysis RFP closed September 30, 2026 with three responses. BED is seeking clarification from all respondents, with material expected back by the end of this week. If there is something to advance, an item could come to the commission at the November meeting.

The Energy Action Network (EAN) Summit occurred, the Renewable Energy Vermont conference was held today, and the Vermont Public Power Supply Authority (VPPSA) Summit in Montpelier also took place. Two commissioners attended the EAN and VPPSA events.

EAN’s Annual Progress Report is available on its website. It is a statewide report with data on affordability, emissions, and energy, and BED is referenced in it. BED holds an internal lunch and learn on it each year.

At Renewable Energy Vermont, Mr. Springer joined a panel on the Renewable Energy Standard, including BED’s Tier 3 strategic electrification programs.

At VPPSA, BED was the largest municipal utility present, which gave it a different perspective than at most statewide events, and he found other municipals’ challenges useful to hear.

The District energy docket (2021 to 2023 spending) closed. The Public Utility Commission found BED had reasonable support for its regulatory basis for the spending, with no adverse action. It was one of the items cited in the commission’s letter last summer.

The ARC business process audit is still awaiting commission action with nothing new to report.

All information requests for the demand resource plan (three-year efficiency budget) are complete, and BED is awaiting commission action. Legislation passed this year allows BED to continue using some TEPF funds through the efficiency utility for emissions reduction and weatherization. Some mild clarifying language may be needed for implementation.

A Tier 3 plan will be submitted by November 1, 2026. BED aims to hold or increase incentives, but state-level studies questioned whether heat pumps are reducing fossil fuel use as intended (for example, use for cooling rather than heating). Changes in regulatory value for heat pumps mean some incentives will likely decrease starting in January, though new, differently structured incentives may still be strong. Leased EV vehicles will have a shorter credit lifespan under Tier 3, reducing their value and the incentive BED can offer. Under Act 97, BED will use TEPF funding to keep the new EV incentive unchanged: $5,000 market rate, $5,700 income qualified, plus up to $300 for high-mileage drivers (up to about $6,000 combined for income-qualified, high-mileage drivers). BED will continue plug-in hybrid and pre-owned vehicle programs. Customers who also buy a Level 2 controllable charger will likely receive a larger incentive. State EV rebates have ended and the federal environment is very unfavorable. Updated incentives will be announced in early January.

Commissioner Kenney asked if the incentive changes were all state-level.

Mr. Springer confirmed that the state Technical Advisory Group (TAG) sets technical qualifications and credit values. Spending limits per credit mean those decisions can raise or lower incentives, and BED has some discretion within that band.

Commissioner Williams asked if there was a timeline for the ARC outcome.

Mr. Springer responded that it is unknown at this time. Dates were submitted for a possible evidentiary hearing, but they have passed and nothing has been scheduled. BED continues to work on the recommendations in the meantime.

## 8. Financials: August FY27

Emily Stebbins-Wheelock, CFO and Manager of Strategy & Innovation, presented August 2026 financial results.

There was a net loss of $272,000 versus a budgeted net income of just under $1.9 million. Most of the variance is timing of REC revenues; they were received in July but budgeted for August, so July came in well above budget and August well below.

Operating expenses were relatively on budget, with small variances in net power supply and other O&M. Sales were on basically spot on budget and major expenses were also very close to budget.

Non-operating income and deductions were $154,000 favorable, mostly from timing of gain or loss on disposition of plant, a non-cash item.

The year-to-date results were a $25,000 positive variance to budget for the two months of the fiscal year so far.

Capital spending was $2.5 million spent year to date: 12% of the full-year budget, mostly in production and distribution.

Cash is about $1.9 million above budget. Debt service coverage ratio is 4.59, with an adjusted ratio of 1.29 for the most recent 12 months. There were 158 days cash on hand, including the line of credit. Cash will dip when the GO bond payment is made in October. The City plans to issue its annual GO bond in December, which had been budgeted for September, creating a timing difference. BED expects to receive an additional $3 million in December.

Commissioner Kenney asked why production was under budget again and if it is expected to reach budget.

Ms. Stebbins-Wheelock responded that production was below budget in July and August and is expected to be above budget in September and October, since it has shifted from the planned timing. The annual fall maintenance outage at McNeil was originally scheduled to start this week and has been pushed to November 1. McNeil will be offline for maintenance in early November, and BED will watch supply and energy prices to decide when to return for the winter run.

Commissioner Vota asked why the fall outage was delayed.

Ms. Stebbins-Wheelock responded that it was due to a combination of factors; vendor and contractor availability, coordination with the Winooski One maintenance outage, and an opportunity to replace the ash-removal grates, which had been ordered and scheduled for spring but the grates arrived early. Replacing them before the winter run is expected to improve reliability.

## 9. Commissioners’ Check-In

There were no topics discussed.

## Adjourn

Commissioner Dawson made a motion to adjourn; the motion was seconded by Commissioner Williams. Vote: 4 ayes 0 nays.

The meeting of the Burlington Electric Commission adjourned at 6:08 p.m.
